title: 3D Atlas: Avery–MacLeod–McCarty DNase Proof & the DNA Information Polymer
question: Why did destroying protein or RNA leave Griffith’s transforming principle intact, whereas DNase abolished bacterial transformation completely?
explanation: Inspecting the 3D B-DNA double helix shows how genetic information is physically stored in the linear sequence of A, T, G, and C nitrogenous bases shielded inside the sugar–phosphate backbone.
limits: Historical fibre model ≈10 bp/turn; relaxed B-DNA commonly ≈10.5. Geometry schematic. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Franklin’s Photo 51, B-DNA Pitch (3.4 nm) & Antiparallel Strands
question: How did diffraction measurements, chemical evidence and model-building together reveal complementary DNA strands and an approximately 2 nm double helix?
explanation: Rotating and exploding the 3D B-DNA double helix from the top and side shows the 2.0 nm constant diameter enforced by purine–pyrimidine Watson–Crick base steps stacked 0.34 nm apart inside antiparallel 5′→3′ and 3′→5′ phosphodiester ribbons.
limits: Historical fibre model ≈10 bp/turn; relaxed B-DNA commonly ≈10.5. Geometry schematic. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Khorana’s Synthetic Triplets & the 64-Codon Genetic Cipher
question: Why are 3-base codons the minimum word length needed for a 4-letter nucleotide alphabet to specify 20 amino acids, and how did Har Gobind Khorana crack the table?
explanation: Inspect the ribosome, tRNA adaptors and emerging chain; the adjoining cipher investigation tests synthetic RNA sequences explicitly.
limits: Standard nuclear genetic code. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: RNA Polymerase Transcription Bubble & 80S Ribosome Translation
question: How does RNA polymerase transcribe a 3′→5′ DNA template into 5′→3′ mRNA, and how do the A, P, and E sites of the ribosome translate it?
explanation: Stepping from the 3D RNA polymerase transcription bubble to the 80S ribosome A–P–E tRNA bench traces a gene from unwound DNA template to growing polypeptide chain.
limits: Coupled transcription bubble and 3-slot ribosomal translation. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: From Primary Amino-Acid Chain to 3D Active Protein Machines
question: How does the linear sequence of amino acids emerging from the ribosome’s exit tunnel dictate the 3D shape of an enzyme, antibody, or ion channel?
explanation: Exploding the 3D 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits exposes the nascent polypeptide chain folding as polar, non-polar, and charged side chains interact.
limits: Nascent chain emergence from the 60S ribosomal subunit. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Structural Comparison of Duplex DNA vs Single-Stranded mRNA
question: Why is double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (with thymine) built for permanent archival storage while single-stranded ribonucleic acid (with uracil) serves as a transient messenger?
explanation: Comparing the 3D B-DNA double helix against the single-stranded mRNA ribbon emerging from RNA polymerase highlights the 2′-OH ribose group, uracil base pairing, and single-stranded flexibility.
limits: Side-by-side duplex DNA and single-stranded mRNA comparison. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Sickle-Cell GAG→GTG Point Mutation & HbS Fibre Polymerisation
question: How can mutating a single adenine to thymine out of 3 billion base pairs alter haemoglobin interactions at low oxygen and potentially distort red blood cells into a rigid sickle?
explanation: Switching the β-globin codon 6 slider from GAG (hydrophilic glutamate) to GUG (hydrophobic valine) in 3D exposes a sticky surface patch on deoxygenated HbS tetramers, causing them to polymerise into 14-stranded stiff rods that warp the erythrocyte.
limits: Single-fibre axial polymerisation inside a deformable erythrocyte mesh. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Silent, Missense, Nonsense & Frameshift Mutation Consequences
question: Why does a base substitution in the third ‘wobble’ position of a codon often leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged, whereas a single base deletion changes the downstream reading frame?
explanation: Comparing the 3D ribosome reading frame with the β-globin point mutation station illustrates how triplet reading frames respond to substitutions versus insertions/deletions.
limits: Same amino-acid sequence does not guarantee no RNA-processing or production effects; these are held fixed here. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Codon Degeneracy & Wobble Base Pairing on the Ribosome
question: Why do six different mRNA codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG) all specify the same leucine residue into a growing protein?
explanation: Select the synonymous HBB example: changed DNA and RNA still specify leucine. RNA processing and production are held fixed here.
limits: A-site tRNA anticodon geometry. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Meselson–Stahl Semiconservative Replication Fork & Okazaki Fragments
question: How do heavy and light DNA strands distinguish competing copying models over two generations?
explanation: Compare heavy, hybrid and light fractions in the Meselson–Stahl station. This follows duplex ancestry, not primers or Okazaki-fragment chemistry.
limits: Unwound Y-fork geometry without trombone loop folding. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Sister Chromatids, Centromere Kinetochores & Chromosome Counting
question: Why does an S-phase replicated chromosome with two sister chromatids still count as one chromosome until protein links are released and sisters separate?
explanation: Inspecting the 3D X-shaped metaphase chromosomes and separating anaphase chromatids clarifies how chromosome count follows centromere number while DNA mass doubles in S-phase and halves in anaphase/telophase.
limits: Representative metacentric chromosome pairs. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Flemming’s Mitotic Spindle, Metaphase Plate & Anaphase Separation
question: How does the bipolar microtubule spindle normally distribute one copy of every chromosome?
explanation: Dragging the mitotic phase slider through Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase in 3D shows kinetochore microtubules aligning X-shaped chromosomes on the equatorial metaphase plate before cohesin cleavage lets motor proteins pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.
limits: Two representative homologous chromosome pairs shown for visual clarity. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Clonal Mitotic Propagation vs Meiotic Recombination in Crops
question: Why does vegetative stem cutting preserve an elite sugarcane or mango genotype intact, whereas growing from seed shuffles parental traits?
explanation: Comparing the 3D Mitosis spindle (genetically identical 2n clones) with the Meiosis I crossing-over tetrad explains the trade-off between clonal uniformity and sexual genetic diversity.
limits: Comparative mitotic vs meiotic division mechanics. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Stem Cell Niche & Waddington Epigenetic Differentiation Landscape
question: If a neuron, an immature red-cell precursor, and a smooth muscle cell carry the exact same DNA genome, how do they become so different?
explanation: Watching pluripotent stem cells roll down the branching valleys of Waddington’s 3D epigenetic landscape illustrates how transcription factors and chromatin marks selectively express lineage-specific genes without deleting DNA.
limits: Three-valley bifurcating potential surface. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Gurdon’s Nuclear Transfer & Yamanaka’s iPSC Reprogramming
question: How did nuclear transfer and cell reprogramming show that specialised cells can retain instructions for other cell types?
explanation: In the 3D Waddington epigenetic landscape, reprogramming pushes a differentiated somatic nucleus back uphill to the pluripotent summit, restoring its capacity to roll down any developmental valley.
limits: Potential-energy landscape representation of epigenetic state. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Meiosis I Homologous Bivalent, Chiasma & Crossing Over
question: How do prophase I crossing over and metaphase I independent assortment generate genetically unique haploid gametes?
explanation: Rotating the 3D homologous bivalent tetrad in Prophase I reveals non-sister chromatids breaking and rejoining at the X-shaped chiasma, swapping maternal and paternal allele segments before Meiosis I and II halve ploidy from 2n to n.
limits: Single chiasma exchange shown on a homologous chromosome pair. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Side-by-Side Mitosis (2n → 2n) vs Meiosis (2n → n) Mechanics
question: What is the key mechanical difference at Metaphase I that makes meiosis halve chromosome number while mitosis preserves it?
explanation: Switching between the 3D Mitosis and Meiosis stations shows individual chromosomes lining up single-file in mitotic metaphase versus paired homologous bivalents lining up side-by-side in meiotic Metaphase I.
limits: Comparative 3D spindle and bivalent views. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Triploid (3n = 33) Bivalent Pairing Failure in Seedless Bananas
question: Why are triploid (3n) Cavendish bananas poorly fertile, while parthenocarpy permits seedless fruit, yet able to grow huge fruit clusters when propagated by suckers?
explanation: Inspecting homologous synapsis in the 3D Meiosis I station shows why three copies of each chromosome cannot pair cleanly two-by-two at Metaphase I, causing unbalanced anaphase segregation and inviable gametes while mitotic sucker growth (2n/3n → 3n) proceeds normally.
limits: Chromosome-sorting schematic: irregular segregation reduces fertility; parthenocarpy separately permits fruit without fertilisation. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

title: 3D Atlas: Mendel’s Monohybrid Probabilities and Sampling Uncertainty
question: Why do Tt × Tt parents give an expected 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt genotype ratio and a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio?
explanation: Compare the expected genotype columns with the four-cell Punnett grid. The cross selector changes between Tt × Tt, Tt × tt and TT × tt. Increasing N reduces the displayed standard error; the columns are expected probabilities, not a fresh random sample.
limits: One locus with complete dominance and equal gamete probabilities. No dihybrid tower, random tosses or guaranteed convergence on every run is shown.

title: 3D Atlas: Homologous Chromosome Pair, Gene Loci & Allelic Variants
question: How can two chromosomes carry matching gene loci but different versions of a gene?
explanation: Inspect the maternal and paternal chromosome rods and their matching locus bands. Homozygotes have matching alleles at a locus; heterozygotes have different alleles. The adjacent family symbols illustrate two carrier parents and an affected child.
limits: Schematic marker bands, not measured chromosome geometry or enzyme concentrations. The family example assumes one autosomal gene, complete expression and no new mutation.

title: 3D Atlas: Diagnostic Test Cross (Dominant Phenotype × Homozygous Recessive)
question: Why does a recessive offspring reveal a hidden allele, while an all-dominant sample cannot prove a parent is homozygous?
explanation: Compare the Tt × tt model (expected 1:1 tall:dwarf) with the known TT × tt model (all tall). A dwarf offspring establishes that the tall parent carried t. A finite all-tall sample supports TT but can occur by chance from Tt; the atlas does not simulate an actual breeding trial.
limits: One locus with complete dominance, equal gamete probabilities and no new mutation. Known parental genotypes generate probabilities; observing finite offspring is a separate inference.

title: 3D Atlas: Autosomal Pedigree Clues and Their Assumptions
question: Within a fully expressed single-gene model, what can an affected child of two unaffected parents reveal?
explanation: Inspect the fixed carrier-parent family Aa × Aa and its affected aa child at the chromosome-and-pedigree station. The Punnett probabilities are 25% AA, 50% Aa and 25% aa for each pregnancy. The chapter’s separate pedigree figure compares dominant and recessive deductions.
limits: One autosomal locus, complete penetrance, no new mutation and reliable relationships. Real clinical pedigrees may include reduced penetrance or new variants; the atlas has no pedigree-mode toggle.

title: 3D Atlas: ABO Alleles and Two Cell-Surface Antigens
question: Why does an AB red blood cell display both A and B antigens rather than a blended intermediate?
explanation: Use the ABO selector (0=A, 1=B, 2=AB, 3=O) to inspect schematic surface antigens. A and B transferases attach different terminal sugars to H-antigen chains. In AB, both products occur on the same cell; a common non-functional O allele adds neither terminal sugar.
limits: Standard ABO model with H-antigen present. Sugar markers are schematic shapes, not molecular scale or antigen-density measurements; rare variants and Bombay phenotype can alter typing.

title: 3D Atlas: Complete Dominance vs Codominance on the Cell Surface
question: Why can one working A allele give Group A, whereas A and B together give Group AB?
explanation: Compare A (selector 0), B (1), AB (2) and O (3) on the cell-surface station. One working A allele supplies sufficient transferase for Group A; A and B together supply both antigen-producing activities. A count of working alleles does not measure an exact enzyme percentage.
limits: Representative surface markers, not measured antigen coating or enzyme doses. The atlas selects one representative genotype per group; standard ABO inheritance is assumed.

title: 3D Atlas: X and Y Chromosomes and an Expected Sex Ratio
question: In the typical XX/XY model, which parent supplies the chromosome that makes a zygote XX or XY?
explanation: Compare the schematic X and Y chromosomes. An egg supplies X, while sperm have expected X and Y proportions of one half each. The chromosome grid in the chapter therefore assigns 50% XX and 50% XY probabilities to each fertilisation; observed birth ratios need not be exactly equal.
limits: Typical XX/XY model and equal fertilisation probabilities; chromosome size is schematic, and variations in sex chromosomes or development are not simulated.

title: 3D Atlas: X-Linked Alleles from Mother to Son
question: Why does the fixed carrier-mother × normal-father model give 50% affected sons but 25% affected children overall?
explanation: Inspect the X/Y station and its fixed offspring bars. Sons receive their X from their mother and Y from their father; half of sons inherit the altered X in this cross. Half of daughters inherit it too and are carriers in the simple recessive model. Use the chapter’s separate cross lab to change parent genotypes.
limits: The atlas bars show one fixed cross, not a rotatable three-generation X-linked pedigree. Some women heterozygous for haemophilia variants have bleeding symptoms; F8 and F9 are separate genes and X-inactivation affects expression.

title: 3D Atlas: The ABO Mechanism Behind the Mumbai Ward Puzzle
question: How do A, B and non-functional O alleles help explain the standard ABO grids in the ward puzzle?
explanation: Inspect the A, B, AB and O antigen patterns, then return to the chapter’s parental Punnett grids. Under the stated two-family standard-ABO assumptions, AB × O excludes an ordinary O child. The separate colour-vision pedigree explains a different clinic puzzle and does not identify the newborns.
limits: The atlas illustrates antigen expression, not clinical identity testing or a full parental-cross search. Records and DNA identity testing would confirm a real assignment; rare ABO variants and H-antigen deficiency require further investigation.

title: 3D Atlas: Variation Before Selection
question: How can inherited differences change which cells contribute to later populations?
explanation: Inspect susceptible and pre-existing resistant cells in an illustrative Petri dish, then compare how a chosen survival pressure changes their fractions.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Mutation Supply and Selection
question: What shows that a resistant variant can exist before exposure?
explanation: The dish represents pre-existing variation. Historical fluctuation tests and replica plating support that possibility; some antibiotics can also increase mutation rates without specifying a useful mutation.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Reproductive Success in a Changing Environment
question: Why can the same inherited variant have different reproductive success when conditions change?
explanation: A chosen two-peak landscape changes with drug pressure. It represents relative reproductive contribution, not a measured moth allele trajectory or an inevitable path toward perfection.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Differential Survival in an Illustrative Culture
question: Can the resistant fraction rise without any new mutation?
explanation: The model starts with990 susceptible and10 resistant cells. A chosen exposure removes susceptible cells more readily; displayed fractions are calculated from survivors, not clinical cure or relapse.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Floating and Dry-Habitat Leaves
question: How do rolled hairy leaves and floating leaves solve different physical problems?
explanation: Inspect a sheltered stomatal pocket and a floating leaf with gas spaces. Floating water-lily leaves have upper stomata and can carry water-repellent wax; fully submerged leaves exchange dissolved gases without stomata.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Structure, Mechanism and Reproductive Benefit
question: How can an inherited structure help under particular environmental conditions?
explanation: Use the leaf cutaways to connect sheltered humid air with lower water loss, and internal gas spaces with buoyancy and gas transport. Other plants and animals have different suites of features.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Choosing Which Variants Reproduce
question: How does choosing breeding parents differ from environmental differences in reproductive contribution?
explanation: The illustrative fitness surface helps distinguish a desirable trait from reproductive success in a specified environment. It does not calculate a historical crop yield or the breeder equation.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

title: 3D Atlas: Fossils and Uncertain Evolutionary History
question: What evidence do fossils preserve, and what requires further inference?
explanation: Compare schematic fossil strata. Sahni described Pentoxyleae in1948 as Jurassic; the relevant Rajmahal deposits were later dated Early Cretaceous. This scene does not infer a DNA clock or prove direct ancestry.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates. Relative genotype contributions are assumed; not measurements for modern patients.

title: 3D Atlas: An Assumed Heterozygote Advantage
question: How can selection maintain a variant harmful in homozygotes?
explanation: Change the assumed AA disadvantage while AS fitness is1 and SS fitness is0.20. The mean-fitness curve and equilibrium illustrate balancing selection in a hypothetical random-mating population.
limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates. Relative genotype contributions are assumed; not measurements for modern patients.

title: 3D Atlas: Illustrative Trophic Production Pyramid
question: Why can a tree invert a numbers pyramid while a consistently bounded production pyramid remains upright?
explanation: Adjust transfer efficiency to compare new biomass production at successive levels. At the stated 10%, tertiary consumers have 0.1% of starting production; other efficiencies give different results. Heat and chemical energy in detritus are distinct outputs.
limits: Tier widths are displayed for inspection. Counts and production are illustrative; use the same area/period and include imported food. This does not prove a maximum food-chain length.

title: 3D Atlas: Energy Accounting and Food-Supply Routes
question: Why can an intermediate livestock conversion reduce food energy supplied from the same harvested crop?
explanation: The chapter’s food-supply example follows harvested edible energy before human digestion: 10,000 kJ directly, or 1,000 kJ after a stated 10% livestock conversion. The atlas pyramid separately follows new biomass production.
limits: The atlas does not calculate actual people per hectare. Crop choice, livestock, feed digestibility, grass/by-products and farming system change the comparison.

title: Linked Model: Carbon Reservoirs and Reused Atoms
question: How do photosynthesis, respiration, burial and combustion move carbon between reservoirs?
explanation: Use the chapter’s carbon-cycle figure to trace carbon forms and reservoirs. The atlas nodule/lake station connects the broader idea of matter movement to microbial nutrient transformations.
limits: The atlas is a nodule/lake schematic, not an interactive global four-box carbon model. Photosynthesis is the main sunlit entry route; chemoautotrophs also fix carbon.

title: 3D Atlas: Root Nodules and Nitrogen Transformations
question: How do fixation, nitrification and denitrification change nitrogen into different usable or gaseous forms?
explanation: Inspect the nodule and its microbes: biological fixation produces ammonia/ammonium. Aerobic nitrification produces nitrite then nitrate; denitrification can reduce nitrate towards N₂. Lightning follows a separate nitrogen-oxide/nitrate route.
limits: A schematic, not a calibrated soil forecast. Fixation initially supplies the legume; uptake, leaching, harvesting and residue return also affect soil nitrate.

title: 3D Atlas: Nutrient Enrichment and Low Oxygen
question: Why can a bloom contribute to low oxygen even though algae photosynthesise?
explanation: Inspect one possible nutrient-enrichment pathway. Producer growth supplies organic matter for decomposers; respiration uses dissolved oxygen. Shading can contribute, sewage organic matter can act directly, and living algae respire by day and night.
limits: Illustrative high/low state, not a compulsory seven-stage sequence or numerical oxygen forecast. Mixing, flow, temperature and night-time respiration matter.

title: Linked Model: Forest Carbon Stocks and Conservation
question: How can clearing a forest change stored carbon and future carbon uptake?
explanation: The chapter’s conservation figure links biomass removal, burning/decay, photosynthetic uptake, habitats and nutrient cycling. Compare these mechanisms with the atlas’s nutrient and ecosystem views.
limits: The atlas has no global-carbon or forest-clearing slider. A local effect depends on subsequent land use, regrowth and the time period.

title: 3D Atlas: Fermenter Conditions and Waste Handling
question: Why must a fermenter control oxygen, nutrients, temperature, pH and waste products?
explanation: Inspect the sparger, impellers, probes and cooling jacket. They support culture conditions while respiratory heat and wastes must be managed; product recovery/processing follows growth.
limits: An illustrative E. coli response near 37 °C, not every microbe’s optimum or a prediction of temperature after a cooling failure.

title: 3D Atlas: Recombinant DNA and Guided Cutting
question: What does compatible-end cloning achieve, and what still has to happen after a Cas9 cut?
explanation: Prepare intron-free insulin coding DNA with bacterial controls; pair compatible ends, seal with ligase and select transformed cells. Recover, process/fold and purify the product; mature insulin has two chains. Cas9 targets suitable DNA near a PAM, and cell repair creates the edit.
limits: Stylised plasmid/Cas9 models, not atomic structures or a promise of exact repair. Different enzymes can make compatible ends, and unintended outcomes require checking.

title: 3D Atlas: Mumbai Environments and a Hypothetical Insulin Vial
question: What explanations fit the fictional site comparisons, and what additional evidence would test them?
explanation: Connect trophic budgets, reused atoms, nutrient enrichment and recombinant protein production. The chapter’s three Mumbai-inspired datasets are illustrative comparisons of separate environments.
limits: Not a single downstream watershed or a measured restoration. Mithi drains to Mahim Creek; Thane Creek is separate. One snapshot cannot establish a time trend or treatment effect.
